finding: The site has no live range for this job, so there is nothing to compare; these are the totals the evidence supports. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2015 Honda Civic about $41-$109; midsize 2015 Subaru Outback about $43-$108; luxury 2015 Acura MDX about $41-$109 (genuine filters $19-$29, and 10 to 30 minutes); truck 2019 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 LD about $36-$139 (filter $16 aftermarket to $59 genuine at list). A supportable range is roughly $40-$110 for most cars and up to about $140 where the genuine filter is dearer. Against the benchmarks: RepairPal's national $91-$114 and Jerry's $78-$106 sit in the upper half of our range, and RepairPal's Honda Civic ($61-$76) figure falls inside it; RepairPal's Silverado 1500 figure ($99-$121) falls inside the truck range. Our low end is below every benchmark because it pairs a discounted online filter with a 10-12 minute time, and few shops bill less than about a quarter to half an hour for any job; treat roughly $60 as the practical floor at a shop. YourMechanic's $186-$246 for an old Acura CL shows the other extreme: a few vehicles need dash or cowl parts removed (trade press lists book times of 0.4 to 0.7 hours for the hardest ones), and those will exceed these totals. Second look on 2026-11-20, what changed: the midsize example moved from the 2016 Honda CR-V to the 2015 Subaru Outback, because Subaru prints a time for it: 0.2 labor hours to fit a cabin filter in a base 2015 Legacy or Outback shipped without one. That is the only maker-stated time found for an example vehicle, and it is for fitting a filter into an empty housing rather than swapping an old one, so it slightly understates a replacement. The Outback's genuine filter ($19.49 discounted, $28.25 list, two sources) costs almost exactly what the Honda one does, so the range barely moves. How solid the labor times are: still weak. For the Civic, Silverado and MDX no maker-stated time was found; their low end is a parts retailer's 10 minutes on a Honda Civic of unstated year or a named technical writer's '10 minutes or less on the easier applications', and every high end is a mechanic-written guide's 15-30 minutes in a shop. New cross-checks, none used as a range end: Honda (2015-20 Fit) and Acura (2014-18 RLX) bulletins allow 0.3 hr for replacing the blower motor whether or not the filter is replaced with it, which points to well under 0.3 hr for the filter alone on those cars; Mopar's own guide says 10 to 20 minutes for most of its vehicles; a 2007 trade article says about 10 minutes for glovebox-access filters. Toyota's and Lexus's HVAC odor bulletins call for replacing the filter but print no labor time; GM's cabin filter bulletins for older Silverados print no labor operation; Hyundai's and Mazda's cabin filter bulletins print none either. The published book times found (0.1-0.7 hours) are for other vehicles. Where the Silverado's filter sits and how long it takes was not checked, and its filter fitment should be confirmed by VIN. No aftermarket filter price was verified for the Outback. No chain price menu with a posted price was found. An estimate is not a quote. Posted menu prices, added 2026-11-20: eight sellers' own pages (two independent shops and six dealers in NC, PA, LA, NJ, NY, GA and HI) post cabin air filter replacement at $35 to $119.95, with five of the eight between about $55 and $63, which sits inside the built range for most cars; no national chain page with a posted cabin filter price was found, so the earlier statement that no posted price was found now applies to chains only.
extras: A quote often adds shop supplies and sales tax, and many shops charge a minimum labor amount that is more than the minutes the job takes. A charcoal (odor) or HEPA filter costs more than the standard element. It is often offered together with an engine air filter, an evaporator cleaning or odor treatment, or clearing leaves from the cowl intake, each quoted separately. A few vehicles have two filter elements or need the glove box, a dash panel or cowl trim removed, which raises the labor.
